canberra.title: After 36 years working with Transport Canberra, Mick has parked the bus for the last time
canberra.snippet: In 36 years with Transport Canberra, Mick Scott has helped millions of Canberrans get around the city. But after a lifetime of service, i...
canberra.content:
Michael ‘Mick’ Scott and his close mate Les Gallagher celebrating their retirement. Photo: Transport Canberra.

In 36 years with Transport Canberra, Mick Scott has helped millions of Canberrans get around the city. But after a lifetime of service, it’s time for Mick to park the bus one last time as he calls time on his near-four-decade career.

Starting his professional life as a panel beater, an ad in the newspaper to rebuild buses first caught Mick’s attention.

After applying, Mick began working on upgrading old bendy/banana buses and replacing doors in the centre of the vehicle with walls and floors.

“A lot of the buses that we refurbished in the day, a lot of them were all done up really nicely. We were very proud of them,” Mick said.

“We kept some, and some were sold to all different parts of Australia, and some went over to New Zealand.

“I worked on them for a few years and then in the late 90s, they [Transport Canberra] were short a few drivers, so I took part in what we called multi-bus driving.

“We would drive during the peak hours in the morning and afternoon, especially to pick up school kids either side of school.”

Throughout the late 90s and early 2000s, Mick would complete several courses and hours of training to become an acting transport officer.

“I would oversee unit changes; I’d work in the radio room and communicate with a lot of the different drivers around the city,” he said.

“For 13 years, I would deal with almost all of the on-road incidents that occurred.”

After his time at the communications centre, Mick became Field Operations Manager for the southside of Canberra, supervising all public transport operations in the city’s southern suburbs.

Mick has seen countless changes to public transport in his time, but he said advancements to buses are among the greatest.

“When I started, there were no wheelchair-friendly buses, and there were no video cameras,” he said.

“Now we’ve got a fully wheelchair accessible bus fleet, and we’ve got CCTV in all our buses. In the 90s there was no air conditioning; a few had fans, but now they’re fully kitted out.

“We now have electronic destination signs as well. That all used to be done manually.

“One of the biggest changes that people don’t think about is power steering. We never used to have that in the old buses. It was quite the exercise.”

Mick isn’t the only long-time Transport Canberra employee calling time. Long-time friend and Field Operations Manager Les Gallagher has also hung up the high-vis after three decades.

Mick said it feels special to end his career alongside Les, a man he has worked with for decades.

“Les and I are very close friends and we’ve covered a lot of big events together,” he said.

“I’ll remember getting up at 2 am for every Anzac Day Dawn Service and every big sporting event. Every one of those things, I had with Les beside me.

“It will definitely take a little bit to get used to waking up and not going to work to see Les, but we’re both really proud of our time at Transport Canberra.”

Now with his well-earned retirement ahead of him, Mick said the biggest thing he will miss, looking back, is the people, both within Transport Canberra and the passengers he supported.

“Funny thing is, I always have people running up to me at the shopping centre saying they remember me driving them,” he said

“A few of them are friends with me on Facebook, and they’re always sending me messages and things like that.

“I’ll also miss all the friendships I made. You meet a lot of different contractors and other drivers along the journey. You become mates with almost all of them.

“While I’d do it all again and I’ll miss everyone, I am excited to spend some more time with my daughters and travel.”

canberra.title: What deserves an emergency call to Triple Zero? Some Canberrans are making mountains out of molehills
canberra.snippet: Canberrans appear confused about what constitutes a real emergency, with frontline agencies pleading with residents to save Triple Zero f...
canberra.content:
Whether you call Triple Zero (000) or the Police Assistance Line (131 444), it’s answered here. Emergency calls are prioritised over calls for assistance. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

Canberrans appear confused about what constitutes a real emergency, with frontline agencies pleading with residents to save Triple Zero for life-threatening situations.

ACT Policing received 57,000 Triple Zero calls last financial year, and data already show a significant increase this financial year.

Chief Police Officer Scott Lee gave examples of calls he felt no one should have confused with a dangerous situation.

“Some of those calls are for food deliveries that are cold, landlords who won’t let tenants use their air conditioning, for no access to Wi-Fi,” he said.

“Now, obviously, these are issues that might be impacting the individual, but they are not Triple Zero calls.

“We really need to ensure that we keep Triple Zero for those life-threatening situations where we need to get police out to help the community.”

Other examples included a person being swooped by a magpie, minor car-park collisions with no injuries, barking dogs and loud parties.

ACT Ambulance Services is also feeling the pressure.

The service received around 20,000 Triple Zero calls in the last quarter. Almost half of those (9,000) were for non-emergencies and didn’t require an ambulance to be dispatched.

ACT Chief Ambulance Officer David Dutton said tying up the emergency line with such calls could be the difference between life and death for someone else.

“I think every paramedic, sadly, has a story about a call to an ingrown toenail – that is not a life-threatening emergency,” he said.

“A life-threatening emergency is someone unconscious, someone who is experiencing chest pain, someone who is experiencing symptoms of a stroke, for example, or suffering perhaps from life-threatening hemorrhage.

“When our Triple Zero call operators are occupied on a call, they’re unavailable to answer the next call.”

Security alarms and cats stuck in trees also aren’t reasons for emergency services to show up with lights and sirens.

“It is a common call, and we’ve got the equipment and the staff that can do it, and we do rescue cats out of trees as part of our legislative responsibility,” ACT Fire & Rescue Commander Adam Garrett said.

“[But] it wouldn’t be an emergency, no.”

The options available to address concerns depend on the scenario.

If the issue is health-related, some people may choose to self-present to the emergency department. Other options include talking to a GP, pharmacist, going to a Walk-in Centre, or calling Health Direct.

“None of us can plan for an emergency, but if we have a family member that’s unwell, we can plan in advance,” Mr Dutton said.

“Are we able to contact our general practitioner? What hours is our local pharmacy open? Would the Walk-in Centre offer some assistance for the particular presentation being experienced? We’re asking people to think in advance.”

If the issue is crime-related, ACT Policing can be contacted on 131 444 or through Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

The general rule is that the Triple Zero line is for emergencies occurring at the time of the call. The other two options are for non-life-threatening or non-time-critical crimes.

It is an offence under ACT and Commonwealth legislation to make a false report to police, to cause police or other emergency service resources to be wasted, or to make harassing phone calls to emergency services.

Those found guilty face up to three years’ imprisonment.

For people who have concerns for their own or someone else’s mental health, contact Access Mental Health on 1800 629 354.

The Triple Zero Kids Challenge is a practical way for families and children to understand when it’s appropriate to call Triple Zero.

Police, Fire and Emergency Services Minister Dr Marisa Paterson said keeping emergency lines available for genuine emergencies was everyone’s responsibility.

“Our emergency call-takers do an incredible job supporting Canberrans during some of the most difficult moments of their lives,” she said.

“Using 000 for non-emergency situations can delay assistance reaching someone who is facing a life-threatening emergency.

“The message is simple: if it’s an emergency, call 000. If it’s not an emergency, choose the service best placed to provide the care you need.”

canberra.title: New Googong release redefines affordable living
canberra.snippet: In many masterplanned developments, small, affordable blocks often sit flat in the middle of the estate, while elevated, multi-million-do...
canberra.content:
Googong’s latest release, Talpa Estate, delivers high-spec, house and land packages with freestanding homes on elevated, low-maintenance hillside blocks at a sub-$1 million price point. Image AI Impression: Village Building Co.

In many masterplanned developments, small, affordable blocks often sit flat in the middle of the estate, while elevated, multi-million-dollar views are reserved exclusively for sprawling luxury builds.

But just 16 km from the Canberra CBD, a planning revolution is taking place at Googong’s Talpa Estate.

Leveraging the natural slope and sweeping northern and eastern vistas toward timbered ridgelines and Googong Dam, The Village Building Co is launching a new product designed to act as a financial release valve for the capital region.

Unlocking a state-level planning provision, Village has effectively halved the traditional 1000 sqm lot standard, creating 500 sqm blocks.

This latest release introduces the estate’s first house-and-land packages, delivering high-spec, three-bedroom freestanding homes on elevated, low-maintenance hillside blocks at a sub-$1 million price point — all without losing the backyard.

The Village Building Co’s Jason Burgess said the “market-leading” design was conceived as a pathway to more achievable family homes.

“With the reasonably tight market, there’s a limited number of people who have the resources to be able to firstly buy a 1000-sqm block and then also put a reasonable house on it,” he says.

“These new blocks offer diverse dwelling options to ensure a continuous ladder for downsizers and first-home buyers alike while keeping the entry-level price point attainable. Yet, they still offer the prestige and outlook of an elevated block.”

New house and land packages at Talpa Estate leverage the natural slope and sweeping northern and eastern vistas toward timbered ridgelines and Googong Dam. Photo: Village Building Co.

Traditional house-and-land packages, including many across the broader Googong area, typically rely on split contracts — one for the land and one for the build. While this approach offers flexibility for custom designs, it usually requires progressive payments throughout construction.

Advertised base prices may also exclude major site costs like retaining walls, earthworks, piers, fencing and landscaping.

Talpa Estate directly addresses both hurdles by selling its packages as single-contract, full-turnkey builds.

“For many, servicing a growing mortgage on an unbuilt house while simultaneously paying rent or an existing mortgage creates significant financial strain,” Jason says.

“Talpa contracts don’t require progress payments — you pay a 10 per cent deposit and then the rest on settlement.”

The fresh offering debuts with standalone energy-efficient modern dwellings. Outside of a small, shared portion of common land reserved for utility services like drainage, each home remains completely independent.

“The rest of their property will be their own property, with its own driveway,” Jason says.

The new packages at Talpa Estate are single-contract, full-turnkey builds. Image: Village Building Co.

Spanning roughly 175 sqm of floor space across two storeys to optimise views, the homes leave ample outdoor room for landscaping and a backyard. To achieve economies of scale, floorplans remain consistent, though buyers can select their preferred interior colour schemes.

The estate’s position, a 25-minute drive into the heart of the capital via major arterial links like the Monaro Highway, eliminates the typical trade-off between affordability and a manageable daily commute.

But buyers are also plugging directly into Googong’s mature, self-contained township.

“Buying into a new estate sometimes feels like a speculative gamble — you’re moving into an isolated dirt patch and waiting years for basic infrastructure to catch up,” Jason says.

“Talpa Estate leverages off all of the amenity and existing infrastructure that has already been part of Googong for the last 10 years. Schools, sports teams, playing fields, playgrounds and a swimming pool are all within walking distance. A landscaped spine runs from Googong Road all the way up to the shops in Googong, just 600 metres away.

“It means residents can have the convenience of the facilities without having to be jammed in with neighbours on every boundary. We call it proximity without isolation.”

For more information, visit Talpa Estate.

Region Media Partner Content

canberra.title: ‘My heart stopped’: Parents alarmed as ACT schools dismiss false absence alerts as ‘minor discrepancies’
canberra.snippet: A Canberra mother was at work when a message from her seven-year-old child’s public school sent her into a panic. It was 10:19 am. ...
canberra.content:
False school absence alerts are leaving Canberra parents panicked and questioning the system’s reliability. Photo: ACT Public Schools.

A Canberra mother was at work when a message from her seven-year-old child’s public school sent her into a panic. It was 10:19 am. The notification said her child had not arrived at school and was marked absent.

But she had dropped the child outside the school herself that morning.

Terrified that something had happened between the school gate and the classroom, she immediately called the school. She was told staff would check and call her back. With no immediate confirmation of her child’s whereabouts, the mother decided to leave work and rush to the school.

It was only while she was on her way that the school called to confirm her child was safely in class.

“Do they realise what a parent can go through when they receive a message like this? For a few minutes my heart stopped beating,” she said.

What initially seemed like an isolated mistake became more concerning when she spoke to other parents. Several told her they had received similar incorrect absence notifications. Some said it had happened more than three times.

For some, the alerts had become so familiar that they no longer caused the same alarm.

“The problem is that we don’t know when to trust these messages,” she said.

False alarms on the Parent Portal warning system are causing grief among parents. Image: Screenshot.

In response to questions from Region, the ACT Education Directorate said all ACT public schools used a central School Administration System to record attendance.

Teachers mark the roll at the beginning of the school day, while front office staff reconcile information about absences, late arrivals, sick bay attendance and students participating in activities outside their usual classrooms before unexplained absence notifications are sent.

However, the Directorate acknowledged that mistakes could still occur.

“While schools undertake administrative checks between morning roll call and sending absence alerts, occasional errors can still occur in busy school environments,” it said.

Possible causes include students arriving late without signing in, moving between split classes or attending support programs on school grounds.

But the explanation raises questions about the safeguards in place for younger children, particularly those in Year 1 or Year 2, who may not be responsible for recording their own movements or correcting administrative mistakes.

The Directorate did not detail any requirement for staff to physically verify a child’s whereabouts across the school grounds before an alert was issued. More concerning is the apparent gap in oversight.

While formal complaints are recorded, the Directorate said “minor administrative discrepancies” resolved directly at schools could not be separated from central reporting.

In other words, the Directorate cannot readily say how many parents have been incorrectly told their children are absent, how frequently the mistakes recur or whether particular schools are experiencing repeated problems.

Without those figures, it is difficult to assess the scale of the issue or whether existing safeguards are working. The Directorate acknowledged the distress caused by incorrect alerts.

“We acknowledge how distressing it is for any parent or carer, particularly those of younger children, to receive an unexpected absence message when they believe their child is safely at school,” it said.

“Same-day notification systems are designed as a vital safety net to quickly alert families when a child has not arrived as expected, and it is essential that families maintain confidence in those alerts.”

But when asked what was being done to reduce false notifications, the Directorate largely pointed to existing procedures, including reminders for families to report absences and ensure late-arriving students signed in at the front office.

It said staff immediately checked a student’s location when contacted by a parent following an absence alert. Where an error occurred, schools updated the attendance record and reviewed the cause to prevent a recurrence.

The response did not identify any new system-wide measures, independent checks or targets to reduce incorrect notifications. The issue is not simply that an attendance record can be marked incorrectly. Mistakes happen.

It is that a system designed to alert parents to a potentially missing child must be reliable enough for those warnings to be taken seriously. For the mother who received that 10:19 am message, the experience was anything but a minor discrepancy.

And the question remains: if her child really had gone missing that morning, how would she have known the difference?

canberra.title: Data centre hysteria threatens Australia’s digital self-sufficiency, warns CDC founder
canberra.snippet: Government should do more to explain the importance of the data centre industry to Australia’s digital infrastructure as it battles...
canberra.content:
CDC founder and CEO Greg Boorer says the data centre industry in Australia is misunderstood. Photos: Ben Appleton/PHOTOX.

Government should do more to explain the importance of the data centre industry to Australia’s digital infrastructure as it battles to overcome rising community concern about the boom sector, leading industry figure Greg Boorer says.

Speaking at an ACT Property Council event on Monday (23 November), the CDC founder and CEO said Australia had a golden opportunity to build its own sovereign capability to take advantage of the advances in artificial intelligence, but the industry was being left to defend itself against misinformation that ironically was being amplified through social media.

Mr Boorer said that, in much the same way as gas, solar, wind and battery technology had been demonised, particularly in the regions, data centres were being opposed on grounds with no factual basis, turbocharged by anxiety about AI.

He said opponents labelled them water and energy guzzlers, even though no CDC data centres in the company’s 20-year history had used water for cooling, and were powered by renewable energy.

They did not inflate power bills, and CDC often underwrote new generation on the grid to offset everything it built.

“We’ve got 20 years of history and experience of working with the community, community consultation, engagement, all of those things, because you’ve got to do that to survive in Canberra,” Mr Boorer said.

He said CDC’s proposed Wagga Wagga data centre would be one of the biggest regional projects in Australia, and the site was selected based on advice from the government and the electricity utility provider that it was the best location in Australia.

Yet CDC was left to defend itself from a small but effective opposition, and do it all itself in terms of community engagement and explaining that the project comes with a $225 million benefit-sharing fund for the city.

“The positive people go that’s fantastic, all the local businesses, that’s fantastic, but they don’t say anything,” Mr Boorer said.

“Whereas you’ve got 90 people on a petition that are going bananas and all they’re raging about is imported, concocted outrage on social media from the United States about gas turbines that we’re not even talking about, and it’s never going to happen in this country, let alone at Wagga.”

Mr Boorer said CDC wanted governments such as the ACT to set as high a bar as possible for developing their data centre industry frameworks because that would formalise everything CDC had achieved in its 20 years.

Greg Boorer and Property Council ACT and Region executive director Ashlee Berry. If data centres stopped working tomorrow, the country would stop.

Australians needed to understand the crucial role that data centres play and would continue to play in the economy and function of a modern nation, not just with AI but government and commerce in general.

“I don’t think the average person realises that they’d probably touch a data centre 10 or 15 times before they even have breakfast every day. Looking at their phone to check the news, to do some messaging, you know, maybe a virtual call with a family member overseas or something like that,” Mr Boorer said.

He said data centres were really important digital infrastructure from a sovereign perspective, and the impacts of the war in the Middle East only reinforced that.

Mr Boorer said the war showed how vulnerable Australia was to external events and if its data centres stopped working tomorrow, the country would stop.

He said you did not want those services in another third-party country.

“We had 30 days to work out the fuel supply issue, whereas with AI, with digital services, they can be turned off in a second,” Mr Boorer said.

Conversely, if other countries were digitally dependent on Australia, imagine the geostrategic and geopolitical levers available to pull when times got tough.

“Australia just needs to have a good think about their position in the world, how wealthy we want to be, how powerful we want to be, and if we do it correctly, which I think we are leading the charge on, then Australia has an enormous role to play in the world,” Mr Boorer said.

He said a slowdown in data centre investment in the US due to the mid-term election results and in the Gulf states due to the war gave Australia an opening for about a decade to develop its own digital infrastructure.

“So Australia suddenly has this amazing opportunity to do really, really well if the data centres are in the right locations, and we’re not talking in the middle of residential estates, we’re talking in hardcore industrial areas or in regional areas with the necessary grid connectivity and communications connectivity,” Mr Boorer said.

“Then we could actually do amazing things, but it’s got to be done correctly, and it’s got to be done well.”

australia.title: Plant-based lunches could cut Australia’s emissions by 15m tonnes, new research shows
australia.snippet: Nationwide change in lunch habits could cut more climate pollution than grounding every domestic flight Get our breaking news email , fre...
australia.content:
Australians could collectively cut climate pollution by more than 15m tonnes – more than grounding every domestic flight – simply by changing what they eat for lunch.

A nationwide shift to plant-based lunches could reduce food-related emissions by 29% – 15.4m tonnes per year – while saving the average household about $611 annually, according to a report by Bryant Research and not-for-profit ProVeg.

Nadia Schilling, the executive director of ProVeg Australia, said the findings highlighted the “huge difference” that relatively modest changes, like a meat-free Monday or a plant-based lunch, could make.

That might mean opting for a black bean burrito, a poke bowl with tofu, or a lunchbox with hummus and fresh vegetables – instead of a cheese and ham wrap – she said.

“We realise that Australians aren’t going to change their diets overnight,” Schilling said. “This is a really practical change where everyone wins. Lunch is a huge missed opportunity.”

Australia has the highest per capita food-related emissions in the world, the report found. It modelled the environmental, health and economic impacts for a range of Australia-wide dietary changes, finding the shift to 100% plant-based meals would cut dietary emissions by two-thirds, while just switching lunches would cut nearly one-third.

Emissions from domestic aviation are about 10m tonnes a year, according to government data.

The organisations behind the report, which promote moving from meat to plant-rich foods and alternative protein sources, called for a national campaign to increase vegetable consumption along with policy and funding support for plant proteins.

Almost one-third of global greenhouse gas emissions are connected to the global food system through land clearing, raising animals, growing crops, processing, packaging, transport and waste.

The National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) is reviewing the evidence about sustainability and diet as part of the first update of Australian dietary guidelines in more than 13 years. Draft guidelines are expected to be released for public consultation in December 2026.

An NHMRC spokesperson said the expert committee drafting the new guidelines had prioritised information on health impacts, but “information about the economic, social, and environmental sustainability of diets was then considered as one of the many factors that influence people’s ability to follow a healthy diet”.

Dr Diana Bogueva, who researches food sustainability at Curtin University, said relatively small changes in everyday eating habits – when adopted by a large number of people – could have a major impact on the environmental footprint of food production.

However, Bogueva, who was not involved with the report, said the environmental, health and affordability benefits of eating less meat depended on what foods replaced it.

Whole foods like legumes, grains, vegetables, nuts and seeds provided valuable fibre, vitamins, minerals and plant proteins, she said. “But not every plant-based product is automatically healthy,” Bogueva said. “Simply swapping meat for highly processed products does not necessarily improve the nutritional quality of the meal.”

Sustainable eating didn’t have to be expensive, she added, and some of the most nutritious sources of plant protein – such as beans, lentils and chickpeas – were also among the most affordable.

“We do know there are both health and environmental benefits if you reduce red and processed meat in your diet,” said Alexandra Jones, an associate professor at the George Institute for Global Health, who was not involved with the report.

But rather than focusing on swapping out one protein for another, the emphasis should be on “helping people eat more vegetables, legumes and minimally processed plant foods,” she said.

A good lunch could be as simple as an “old-school salad sandwich” on wholegrain bread, with lettuce, tomato, sprouts and beetroot.

australia.title: Domestic violence perpetrators are misusing smart car features to abuse, researchers warn
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Alarming report reveals how tracking and monitoring functions and digital key access have been used to facilitate abuse Get ou...
australia.content:
Earlier this year a man in Australia was found guilty of using a connected car app to harass his former partner, including restricting the speed at which she could drive, sometimes to 40km an hour.

In 2022 in the US, a woman found her former husband had used a car app associated with her car to track her; the carmaker then allegedly refused to terminate the former partner’s digital access to the vehicle.

In another case in the US in 2020, a woman found a baseball bat her former partner had used to threaten her in the back seat of her car.

These three cases form part of an alarming report by University of New South Wales researchers, released on Tuesday, which warned this was an emerging problem that could get worse. It found smart car functions that could be misused by perpetrators of domestic violence to facilitate abuse were prevalent across major car brands.

“There is an urgent need for carmakers to adopt safety by design principles from the early stages of designing both the apps and the cars,” said the report co-author Katharine Kemp, a data privacy and consumer protection expert at UNSW.

The researchers found that problems emerged as many of the cars’ functions – which include tracking and monitoring functions, remote control functions and digital key access – could be controlled remotely via an app.

The researchers said that there were three main scenarios that could open the functions to misuse: the abuser being the owner of the car and having created the account themselves; they were granted access as a secondary user of the car; or the victim survivor is impersonated and the perpetrator creates an account on their behalf.

The report said that the problematic functions are mainly marketed by the car manufacturers as being for the purpose of enabling the car owner to “keep an eye on” and protect their car.

It highlighted an advertisement on the carmaker Kia’s Australian website for “Kia Connect”. Kia was contacted for comment.

“Kia Connect is also bundled with geofence and time fencing alerts which let the owner know when another user strays outside preset limits of geographical areas or time limitations. It’s a perfect feature for anyone dealing with a family member who is borrowing the car,” the advertisement said.

The report mapped how prevalent potentially problematic functions were, and whether these functions were advertised by 15 of the top car brands.

One of the functions raised was geolocation, which allows the geographical location of the car in real-time or when it is parked, and was advertised by 100% of the 15 car brands, with some marketing it as “Vehicle Tracking”, “Vehicle Locator” or “Find My Car”. The researchers said this tool could be misused to track people.

The researchers found that 60% of the top 15 brands also advertised a “zone exit alert” which allows users to set an alarm if a car leaves a designated area. They warned this functions could be used to: “Set a zone of 3km from the family home to receive alert if the victim-survivor attempts to leave or fails to follow abuser’s rules limiting travel by the victim-survivor.”

Meanwhile, 20% advertise speed or acceleration restrictions. The explanation of this function by carmakers includes that it is to set speed limits for young drivers or valet parkers.

But the report warned this could be misused to set a speed limit of 40km/h so that a victim survivor cannot safely use highways or escape at speed.

The researchers also raised concerns about digital key access, which allows drivers to use their mobile phone to unlock the car or start the engine and was advertised by 67% of car brands in the Australian market. The report warns: “This function may also allow an abuser to remotely terminate or severely restrict the victim survivor’s ability to use the vehicle.

“An abuser can achieve this, for example, by remotely deactivating the victim-survivor’s digital key access or setting speed restrictions on the vehicle. This could effectively strand the victim-survivor in an unsafe location and/or limit the victim survivor’s ability to escape the abuser’s violence,” the report said.

‘Almost no accountability’ for manufacturers

Emma Buxton-Namisnyk, a co-author of the report, warned this was an emerging problem that could get worse.

“There’s really not a widespread understanding about how these technologies can be misused,” she said, adding that there was “almost no accountability” for car manufacturers to limit potential misuses.

The report recommended carmakers adopt principles which consider at the design phase how a function could be misused to facilitate abuse, and help determine if a function should not be offered because the risks outweigh the benefits.

Last year the eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, raised the alarm on the issue after receiving reports from frontline workers that cars were being used to monitor and track victim-survivors of domestic violence.

She called for improved industry safeguards, noting that it was estimated that more than 90% of new cars sold in Australia by 2031 would have embedded connectivity.

“We need urgent action to make them safer,” Inman Grant said.

The minister for social services, Tanya Plibersek, said in a statement to Guardian Australia that the government was considering what more it could do to crack down on the risk posed by smart devices, after developing a support service on technology-facilitated abuse that helps frontline workers navigate the issue.

“We’re seeing new frontiers of family and domestic violence emerge every day – we’ve seen smart fridges, cat feeders and electric vehicles all being weaponised to stalk, control and harm,” she said.

“We’ll consider what more we can do as we finalise our Second Action Plan to End Violence Against Women and Children.”

australia.title: ‘They will never be forgotten again’: uncovering the buried history of Australia’s enslaved South Sea Islanders
australia.snippet: The descendants of the thousands ‘blackbirded’ to work and die on Queensland farms and plantations say the truth about the country’s prac...
australia.content:
Uncle Graham Tanner’s great-grandfather was enslaved.

Harry Tanner was born in 1855 on Tanna Island in Vanuatu and abducted to work in Queensland’s sugar plantations under a practice known as blackbirding.

Neither Harry nor his son Robert – Graham Tanner’s grandfather – had any rights or recognition as Australian residents. Arthur James “Hobie” Tanner, Graham’s father, was described on his unofficial birth certificate as the son of a slave.

“Us guys are that close. Our dads had this,” he says. “Islanders were slaves, buried where they dropped.”

Leaning across a table that overlooks the river in the Queensland port city of Bundaberg, one of the hubs of the nation’s sugar industry – and of blackbirding – Tanner can see his family’s history.

Between the 1860s – the decade the emancipation proclamation was signed in the United States – and the 1910s, at least 62,000 Pacific Islanders were coerced, tricked or kidnapped to provide labour on Australian sugar cane plantations. Hidden in the humid north, the use of indentured workers spread.

The term “blackbirding” to describe this practice was taken from the transatlantic slave trade. At least 15,000 Islanders died on the cane fields, succumbing to overwork, malnutrition or exposure to diseases brought to Australia from Europe. The mortality rate was about 25%.

Australia’s history of slavery is rarely mentioned. But for the descendants of those taken, the Australian South Sea Islander (ASSI) community, this dark past is held close, buried beneath paddocks in thousands of largely unmarked graves.

Sunnyside

Just outside Bundaberg is Sunnyside, a former sugar plantation owned by the family of former federal Labor MP Brian Courtice for more than a century.

Down the driveway is a stately old home in the high-stumped Queenslander style alongside two ancient weeping fig trees. About 30 metres from the veranda is a rectangular patch of buffalo grass, framed by a timber fence. The air hums with insects and birdsong.

Beyond the fence, red-dirt paddocks, leased for sweet potatoes, stretch toward the horizon. And beneath the buffalo grass, shaded by the reaching branches of the trees, lie the remains of 29 South Sea Islanders.

Courtice’s grandfather and great-uncle bought the property in 1922, two decades after the blackbirding era ended.

“The past had already been completely sanitised,” Courtice says. “If it wasn’t for the old farmers telling my grandfather that they used to see freshly dug graves when they hauled their drays through here, no one would have ever known.”

In 2013, Courtice arranged for a local cemetery worker to use a ground-penetrating radar to survey the plot.

“She walked it up and down,” he says. “Then she stopped, got out the can of spray paint, and started marking rectangles in the grass. Thirteen in the front row. Ten in the second. Six in the third. When she got to the fourth grave in the front row, she looked up and said: ‘That’s a child … It’s a small grave.’”

The burial ground was added to the Queensland heritage register that year, 150 years after the trade began. Despite the scans revealing 29 graves, the plantation’s original owner had only officially registered seven deaths. Reading the seven registered names, the then Solomon Islands prime minister, Gordon Darcy Lilo, who attended a recognition ceremony for the graves, identified that three likely came from New Caledonia, two from the Solomons and two from Vanuatu. The remaining 22, including the child, remain nameless.

The two towering fig trees were also listed that year, while the dry-rubble boundary wall at Sunnyside – built by enslaved people – had been heritage listed since 1996.

“Oral history passed down through the Islander community says a man was hanged from that branch after an altercation,” Courtice says, sitting in the trees’ shade.

“There would be thousands buried in Bundaberg where the big plantations were like Fairymead and Bingera,” he says. “There would be thousands buried in Mackay, in Innisfail, in Cairns, in Maryborough.”

The true number of those who died may never be known, Ryan Butta, a historian and author, says.

“Death certificates were often not used because the man or woman was never taken to hospital,” he says. “So those deaths go unrecorded.”

Building the landscape

From the summit of the Hummock – an extinct volcanic crater rising above Bundaberg’s flat coastal plain – the land is a patchwork of green, brown and yellow paddocks. Cane stalks rustle in the sea breeze and tractors and cane trains rumble along Fairymead Road, named for one of the biggest plantations in the region. It’s now home to Bundaberg Sugar.

The physical labour of generations of South Sea Islanders is etched across the terrain. Miles of dry-rubble walls, hand-stacked from volcanic basalt rocks cleared from the red soil, line the fields.

Down on the coast, the same stones form the Bargara basin, a sheltered tidal pool built by hand by South Sea Islanders so white townsfolk could swim, safe from the choppy waters and sharks of the open ocean. The rocks have sat there so long they are now carpeted with curling green mangroves.

“My grandfather was one of the people who built the basin … one of a hundred,” says Aunty Alice Long, a Bundaberg ASSI elder. Her grandfather, Vira Long, was abducted from Longana village on Ambae Island in Vanuatu and renamed Robert.

“Imagine how long it would take to build,” Long says. “A couple of people would have picked the big rocks up together.”

A plaque at the basin says that employers paid 10 shillings for each blackbirded labourer and were required to cover the £10 fee for return passage after a three-year period of indentured servitude was up. Those rules were poorly enforced.

Out of necessity, blackbirded labourers forged a common tongue, blending island dialects with English to create Bislama, a pidgin dialect now commonly used in Micronesia and Melanesia.

“That language was formed here in Bundaberg,” says Tanner.

A brutal practice

Sunnyside was established 1875 by Edward Turner, whose brutality is preserved in court archives. Turner was prosecuted by Polynesian labour inspector William Corfield for starving his workers – dividing 1lb (450g) of meat a day between 11 men and feeding them rotten potatoes which a magistrate deemed “unfit for pigs”.

Turner was also convicted of assaulting a woman named Raincomb, who had been taken from Ambrym Island in Vanuatu.

Labourers on Sunnyside weren’t provided accommodation and had to build shanties from dried cane refuse. “One of the ways they circumvented the British anti-slave laws was to let them have Sunday off,” Courtice says.

“Plantation owners paid a recruitment and shipping fee of just one or two pounds. An islander was worth less than a draught horse. If four or five died in a season, you simply ordered another boatload from the New Hebrides [a colonial name for Vanuatu].

“They were worked until their bodies broke, starved on rations unfit for animals, and when they died, they were buried in the paddock like livestock.”

A dark trade

Australia’s sugar boom was forged in the shadow of abolition.

Even after Britain technically abolished slavery in the colonies 1833 and paid compensation to 46,000 slave owners for the loss of their human “property”, colonial capital flowed into the Pacific. The unmarked graves at Sunnyside show that the abuses of plantation labour were not limited to the West Indies or the American South, Butta says. “They are evidence that these abuses happened here.”

Louis Hope, a Queensland sugar pioneer, came from a prominent slave-owning and slave-trading family, while the Fairfax family – proprietors of the Sydney Morning Herald until the 1990s– were major shareholders in the Colonial Sugar Refining Company (CSR).

At the same time, First Nations people across Australia were forced into unpaid domestic servitude, pastoral work and the perilous pearling industry.

When Australia federated in 1901, the new commonwealth moved to entrench the White Australia policy, ordering the mass deportation of Pacific Islander workers. Some avoided deportation by walking or swimming across into northern New South Wales, joining a community of escaped workers.

The terror of abduction was passed down through generations. When a replica colonial schooner visited the river in Bundaberg, Long climbed down into the cramped hold where captives had been confined – a visceral glimpse into what her ancestors endured.

Asked how she responds to the national myth that Australia never had slavery, Long says: “I just laugh.”

Those who remained in Bundaberg after the deportation push were shut out from white society. Prevented from buying or renting homes in town, families took refuge in the bush along Dr Mays Road in an area known as Moke’s Scrub.

To survive, families lived “the island way,” Long says, cultivating tropical fruits.

“Our people lived in that bush, our grandparents, all along this big long creek,” says Uncle Joe Nagas, an elder who recently returned to his home town of Bundaberg. “When they came out of the scrub, the only way they could get a house was to go to the farmer and work for them, and the farmer paid them back with a bit of property.

“They knew they were good workers … cane cutting was the best money they could get, even after blackbirding.”

His father, Gordon Nagas, was a preacher who managed to buy five acres in the 1950s.

“Not many dark people owned land back in the 50s,” he says. “Now the grandchildren go up there at Christmas time and there’s full mango trees because they planted them years ago.”

Until 1941, South Sea Islanders were banned from burial within the main grounds of Bundaberg cemetery, relegated to a separate plot in the back.

Adjacent to that plot stands the South Sea Islander church and hall complex. The timber buildings were saved from demolition at Fairymead plantation in the 1990s after a community-led legal fight.

Pastor Bruce Little leads the way behind the hall to a shaded plot dotted with white timber crosses and a memorial stone.

Like many in the ASSI community, Little carries dual heritage: his mother was a South Sea Islander from Joskeleigh, Queensland, with ancestors taken from a Vanuatu island, while his father was Aboriginal.

His Aboriginal grandmother, a Wakka Wakka woman, was forcibly removed from her country with her children and sent to Cherbourg mission while her husband was out working.

“Growing up in Emerald, we had to walk on the opposite side of the street from white folks,” he says. “At the pictures, blacks sat on one side, whites on the other.”

This segregation continues today in the telling of history, Tanner says.

“What we want is for this nation to understand that the multibillion-dollar agricultural wealth of this state was built on our ancestors’ backs,” he says. “Fly our flag on the national register. Teach the truth in the schools so our kids don’t get told their history never happened.

“We don’t want pity,” he adds. “Our elders survived kidnapping, starvation and exile, and they passed on strength and dignity to us.”

In 2021, the Bundaberg regional council issued an official apology for the district’s role in blackbirding. Mayor Helen Blackburn says the physical imprint of that era remains visible in the volcanic rock groynes, built by South Sea Islanders to protect the coast.

“They’re part of our fabric,” she says.

Courtice and others are also pushing for an apology to South Sea Islanders from the Australian high commission.

At Sunnyside, the morning sunlight filters through the branches of the poinciana trees that Courtice planted to shelter the dead, casting long shadows across gravesite.

“These 29 South Sea Islanders are buried in the red soil of Sunnyside, my parents and my sister are buried in the red soil of Sunnyside,” Courtice says, gesturing to three headstones on the other side of the house. “And my wife and I are going to be buried here in the same red soil just over there.

“These 29 people died thousands of miles from home, with no family to mourn them.

“As long as my family owns this ground, they will never be forgotten again.”

world.title: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
world.snippet: Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship Europe live – latest up...
world.content:
Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.

Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.

“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.

Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.

In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”

Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.

The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge – a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic seaport of Kaliningrad.

Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The Institute for the Study of War said the Merkury had stopped over for several days, under a cooperation agreement, to refuel and resupply as it escorted Russian cargo ships that could carry military supplies en route to Russia.

The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.

Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.

At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.

Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.

Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts to use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.

More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.

The confirmation that Ukraine was behind the attacks was condemned by the UN-recognised government in Tripoli. It said Libya rejected ⁠any foreign ⁠military ​operations on its territory or in its waters.

There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”

Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.

In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.

Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.

Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, said Ukraine’s strikes in the Mediterranean “were exceptionally brazen and provocative”.

He added: “The question now is how Russia will retaliate,. Perhaps even more pressing is how the [Hafter] family will respond, given how traumatic the scale of the destruction has been for eastern Libyan authorities.”

Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer

world.title: Russian warship sinks in Benghazi after suspected Ukrainian drone attack
world.snippet: No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia A Russian warship docked in th...
world.content:
A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel.

The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government.

Initial reports said several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, triggering the explosion, the officials told the Associated Press.

Satellite imagery showed the Merkury had sunk after the attack, which took place in the Mediterranean, more than 1,000 miles from south Ukraine, marking a notable geographic expansion of the now near five-year war.

Though Ukraine began the war with no navy, it has developed a sea drone capability that threatened Russian warships in the Black Sea. The Russian fleet has been forced to retreat to the eastern port of Novorossiysk because Sevastopol in occupied Crimea had become unsafe.

Hours later, a Russia-linked cargo ship said to be carrying military supplies, the Ascalon, was hit by a sea drone off the coast of Benghazi. Video showed the drone heading directly towards one end of the vessel, again causing a huge explosion.

Libyan naval forces ‌rescued the vessel’s crew, the ‌sources added. The health ministry said some crew members were in stable condition with minor injuries. The number of injured and their nationalities are not known.

Benghazi is controlled by the self-styled Libyan National Army, led by Gen Khalifa Haftar, which controls eastern and southern Libya and has been aligned with Russia.

There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range attacks against Russia far beyond the frontlines.

The UN mission in Libya (Unsmil) expressed “serious concern” over the two drone attacks off Benghazi and called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”, in a post on X.

The ‌eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that ​normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.

It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and ⁠a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take ​legal and ​diplomatic measures against ​anyone found responsible.

“The Libyan government will not ​allow Libyan ‌ports, territory or territorial ​waters ​to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.

The specialist website Naval News earlier identified the ship attacked as the Merkury, a Russian corvette – the smallest class of warship, smaller than a frigate – and said it had almost certainly been destroyed.

HI Sutton, a naval analyst, said the attack was probably conducted by sea drones, after a photograph of one emerged apparently taken off the Libyan coast. The drone, he said, “is also likely the type used in the subsequent attack”. Similar-looking drones were involved in the subsequent attack on the Ascalon cargo ship.

If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the almost five-year war.

But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians on another continent and the working of the port.

A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.

Russian ships regularly make use of the port, which has a growing military importance to the Kremlin, to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean since the country lost its bases in Syria.

Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was ⁠struck by drones in the ⁠Baltic Sea continued to smoulder ​on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.

The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II ⁠on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly ⁠injured.

On Sunday, visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said.

The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials. Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory.

The risk of ⁠further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled ​out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public ​broadcaster ERR on Sunday.

Finland’s military said last ​week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.

world.title: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
world.snippet: Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded Multiple coastal hazard warnings we...
world.content:
Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.

After a yellow level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

world.title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
world.snippet: The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits Environmentalists in South Afri...
world.content:
Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.

The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.

The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.

Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”

Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.

“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.

The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.

Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.

“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”

Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.

The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”

Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.

The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.

A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.

Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

world.title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
world.snippet: Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds One in four women around ...
world.content:
One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.

“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”

The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.

“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.

He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.

In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.

Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.

Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”

She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.

“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”
